questions.question: In projectile motion, which of the following remains same ?
questions.explanation: During projectile motion (neglecting air resistance), the acceleration due to gravity remains constant in both magnitude and direction (always downward). The speed and velocity both change over time. Hence: Answer: (Acceleration)

questions.question: Acceleration of a particle under projectile motion at the highest point of its trajectory is:
questions.explanation: For a typical projectile (assuming only gravity, no air resistance), the only acceleration is due to gravity, which remains gg downward at every point of the trajectory, including the highest point. Answer: The acceleration magnitude is gg.

questions.question: The velocity of a projectile at the initial point {A} is (2 {i}+3 {j}) {m} / {s} . Its velocity (in {m} / {s} ) at point {B} is
questions.explanation: In projectile motion (neglecting air resistance), the horizontal component remains constant, and the vertical component reverses sign when landing at the same level. Thus, an initial velocity of ⟨2, 3⟩ 2,\,3 becomes ⟨2, −3⟩ 2,\,-3 at the landing point.

questions.question: A ball is projected with a velocity 10 ms-1 at an angle of 60° with the vertical direction. Its speed at the highest point of its trajectory will be
questions.explanation: Angle with vertical =60∘,initial speed =10 m/s.{Angle with vertical }=60^, {initial speed }=10\,{m/s}. At launch: Vertical component =10cos⁡60∘=10×12=5 m/s=1060^=1012=5\,{m/s}. Horizontal component =10sin⁡60∘=10×32=53 m/s=1060^=10{√(3)}{2}=5√(3)\,{m/s}. At the highest point, the vertical component becomes zero, while the horizontal component remains unchanged at 53 m/s5√(3)\,{m/s}. Thus the speed there is 53 m/s5√(3)\,{m/s}.

questions.question: Two bodies are projected with the same speed, if one is projected at an angle of 30^{} and the other at an angle of 60^{} to the horizontal, the ratio of the maximum heights reached is:
When do we get maximum height in a simple projectile motion?
questions.explanation: The maximum height is given by H=u²sin⁡2θ2g.H = u² ²/2g. This is maximum when sin⁡2θ² is maximum, i.e. when sin⁡θ=1 = 1 (which happens at θ=90∘ = 90^). Answer: When θ=90∘ = 90^

questions.question: Two bodies are thrown at an angles of 45^{} and 60^{} respectively, with the horizontal. If both bodies attain same vertical height, then the ratio of velocities with which these are thrown is:
questions.explanation: For the first body at 45∘45^, maximum height is H1=v12 sin⁡245∘2g=v12 122g=v124g.H_1 = v_1²\,² 45^/2g = v_1² \,12/2g = v_1²/4g. For the second body at 60∘60^, maximum height is H2=v22 sin⁡260∘2g=v22 342g=3 v228g.H_2 = v_2²\,² 60^/2g = v_2²\,{3/4}{2g} = 3\,v_2²/8g. Since H1=H2H_1 = H_2, v124g=3 v228g  ⟹  v12:v22=32  ⟹  v1v2=32.v_1²/4g = 3\,v_2²/8g \;\; v_1² : v_2² = 3/2 \;\; v_1/v_2 = √(3/2). Thus, the ratio of their launch speeds is 32.√({3){2}}.

questions.question: If a projectile is fired at an angle with the vertical with velocity u , then maximum height attained is given by
questions.explanation: If the projectile is fired at angle θ with the vertical, then its vertical component of velocity is u cos⁡θu\,. The maximum height reached is H=(u cos⁡θ)22 g=u² cos⁡2θ2 g.H = (u\,)²/2\,g = u²\,²/2\,g.

questions.question: If angles of projection are (π/4+) and (π/4-) where <π/4 , then the ratio of horizontal ranges described by the projectile is (projection speed is same) ;
For angle of projection 20^{} , range of a projectile is R . For the same range, another angle of projection should be

questions.question: The motion of a projectile is described by the equation y=a x-b x² . The range of projectile is
questions.explanation: We have y=a x  −  b x².y = a\,x \;-\; b\,x². At the start, x=0⇒y=0x=0 y=0. For the projectile’s landing, again y=0y=0. Solve: a x−b x²=0⟹x(a−b x)=0⟹x=0  or  x=a/b.a\,x - b\,x² = 0 x(a - b\,x) = 0 x=0 \;{or}\; x=a/b. Hence, the range is a/b{a}{b}.

questions.question: The speed of a projectile at its maximum height is half of its initial speed. The angle of projection is
A projectile is fired with velocity u at angle with horizontal. When the particle makes an angle with the horizontal, its speed becomes v, v is given by
For an object thrown at 45° to horizontal, the maximum height (H) and horizontal range (R) are related as:
questions.explanation: For a projectile launched at 45∘45^: Maximum height: H=u²sin⁡245∘2g=u²(12)2g=u²4g.H = u² ² 45^/2g = u²({1/2)}{2g} = u²/4g. Horizontal range: R=u²sin⁡90∘g=u²g.R = u² 90^/g = u²/g. Thus, R=4H.R = 4H.

questions.question: A large number of bullets are fired in all directions with same speed v . What is the maximum area on the ground on which these bullets will spread ?
questions.explanation: When fired at all angles with the same speed vv, the greatest horizontal distance a projectile can travel (the radius of the “spread”) is the maximum range R=v²gR = {v²{g}. Hence, on level ground, all bullets land within a circle of radius RR. Its area is πR²=π(v²g)2=π v⁴g².π R² = π({v²{g})² = π\,v⁴/g².

questions.question: A man fires a large number of bullets in all directions with same speed u. The maximum area on the ground on which these bullets will spread is-
questions.explanation: The maximum horizontal range for a bullet fired with speed u (neglecting air resistance) is Rmax=u²g If bullets are fired in all directions in a horizontal plane, the region on the ground where they land is (to first approximation) a circle of radius Rmax. Hence the area is πRmax2 =  π(u²g)2  =  π u⁴g².

questions.question: If R is the maximum horizontal range of a particle, then the greatest height attained by it is
questions.explanation: Relate Initial velocity to maxium height. The formula for the maximum height h attained by the projectile is given by: h=u²sin²θ2g Again, substituting θ = 45° h=u² sin²45°2g=u²1222g =u² ⋅122g=u²4g Substitute u2 from the range formula: From the range formula, we have u2 = Rg Substituting this into the height formula: h=Rg4g=R4 Final Result: Therefore, the greatest height h attained by the projectile when the maximum horizontal range R is given is h=R4

Equation of motion of a projectile is
questions.explanation: For a projectile launched at speed uu making an angle θ with the horizontal, the standard trajectory equation (neglecting air resistance and taking the launch from the origin) is: y  =  x tan⁡θ  −  g x²2 u² cos⁡2θ.y \;=\; x\, \;-\;g\,x²/2\,u²\,².

questions.question: The motion of a projectile is described by the equation y=a x-b x² . The range of projectile is
questions.explanation: We have y=a x  −  b x².y = a\,x \;-\; b\,x². At the start, x=0⇒y=0x=0 y=0. For the projectile’s landing, again y=0y=0. Solve: a x−b x²=0⟹x(a−b x)=0⟹x=0  or  x=a/b.a\,x - b\,x² = 0 x(a - b\,x) = 0 x=0 \;{or}\; x=a/b. Hence, the range is a/b{a}{b}.

questions.question: For ground to ground projectile motion equation of path is y (m)=12 x-(3/4) x² . Given that {g}=10 {~ms}^{-2} . What is the range of the projectile?
questions.explanation: The trajectory equation is y=12x  −  34 x².y = 12x \;-\;{3}{4}\,x². For a ground‐to‐ground path, at landing y=0y=0. Thus: 12x−34x²=0⟹x(12−34x)=0⟹x=0  (launch)  or  x=16.12x - {3}{4}x² = 0 x(12 - {3}{4}x) = 0 x=0 \;{(launch)}\;{or}\; x=16. Hence the range is 16 m16\,{m}.

questions.question: In a projectile motion, the height y and distance x are given by y = 4t – 5t2 and x = 3t. The acceleration due to gravity is given by
questions.explanation: To find the acceleration due to gravity (g) in the given projectile motion equations, we use the equation for vertical motion: y=4t−5t²y = 4t - 5t² In this equation, the coefficient of t²t²term represents 12g1/2g in the formula y=ut−12gt²y = ut - 1/2gt². Here, gg is the acceleration due to gravity. Given: −5=−12g-5 = -1/2g Solving for gg: 12g=51/2g = 5 g=10g = 10 So, the acceleration due to gravity is 10 units.

questions.question: A body is thrown horizontally from the top of a tower of height 5 {~m} . It touches the ground at a distance of 10 {~m} from the foot of the tower. The initial velocity of the body is: (g=10 {~ms}^{-2})
questions.explanation: Time to fall from height h=5h=5 m (under g=10g=10 m/s²): t=2hg=2×510=1=1 s.t = √({2h){g}} = √({25){10}} = √(1) = 1\,{s}. Horizontal distance covered is 10 m in that 1 s, hence initial horizontal speed: ux=101=10 m/s.u_x = 10/1 = 10\,{m/s}.

questions.question: A bullet is dropped from the same height when another bullet is fired horizontally. They will hit the ground
questions.explanation: Under uniform gravity and neglecting air resistance, the vertical motion of both bullets is identical (both start from rest vertically). Hence, they land together. Answer: Simultaneously.

questions.question: A bomb is released from a horizontal flying aeroplane. The trajectory of bomb is
questions.explanation: When dropped from a horizontally flying plane (assuming no air resistance), the bomb’s horizontal velocity remains constant while it accelerates downward under gravity. This produces a parabolic path in the ground‐observer’s frame. It follows a parabola.

questions.explanation: For vertical throw: H=u²2g=40H=u²/2g=40 So, u²=80gu²=80g Maximum horizontal range: Rmax=u²g=80gg=80 m

questions.question: A projectile fired with initial velocity u at some angle θ has a range R. If the initial velocity be doubled at the same angle of projection, then the range will be
If the initial velocity of a projectile be doubled, keeping the angle of projection same, the maximum height reached by it will
During projectile motion, acceleration of a particle at the highest point of its trajectory is
The maximum range of a projectile is 22 {~m} . When it is thrown at angle of 15^{} with the horizontal, its range will be-
questions.explanation: Given the maximum range Rmax =22 m at θ=45° we use the formula Rmax =v²g to find the initial velocity v. Rearranging the formula, we get v²=Rmax⋅g Substituting Rmax=22 m and g=9.8 m/s2 we get v²=22×9.8=215.6. Thus, v=215.6≈14.68 m/s. Now, we calculate the range R at θ=15° using the formula R=v²sin(2θ)g Substituting v=14.68 m/s,θ=15°, and g=9.8 m/s2, we get R=(14.68)2sin30°9.8. Since sin30°=0.5, we have R=215.6×0.59.8=107.89.8=11 m

questions.question: A car starts from rest and accelerates at 4 m/s2 for 5 seconds. The car then decelerates at 2 m/s2 for the next 4 seconds. What is the total distance traveled by the car?
A particle moves in a straight line under a variable acceleration a(t)=-3t²+4 . What is the velocity of the particle at t = 3 seconds if the initial velocity is 10 m/s ?
questions.explanation: Velocity is the integral of acceleration: a(t)=-3t²+4v = ∫adt = ∫(-3t²+4)dtv = -3t³3 + 4t + C = -t³ + 4t + CAt t = 0, v = 10Therefore, C = 10Now, v at t = 3 s= -27 + 12 + 10 = - 5 m/s Therefore, the velocity is (a negative velocity indicating the particle is moving in the opposite direction).

questions.question: Assertion : A packet is dropped from rising balloon. The initial velocity of packet is zero. Reason : Initial velocity of a dropping packet is equal to the velocity of the body from which it is dropped.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
Assertion (A) is true but (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false but (R) is true.
questions.explanation: When an object is “dropped” from a moving platform, it initially shares the platform’s velocity. Thus if a balloon is rising at some nonzero speed vv, a packet dropped from it initially has that same upward speed vv, not zero. Therefore: Assertion “Initial velocity of packet is zero” is false Reason “Initial velocity of a dropping packet equals the velocity of the body from which it is dropped” is true Hence, the correct choice is the one that says (A) is false but (R) is true.

questions.question: A body A is going from South to North and body B is going from West to East with identical velocity. Then direction of relative velocity of A with respect to B is:
questions.explanation: The correct answer is option A Explaination To find the direction of the relative velocity of body A with respect to body B, we can use the concept of vector subtraction. Let's denote the velocities of bodies A and B as vectors: Velocity of A, v⃗A{v}_A, is directed from South to North. Velocity of B, v⃗B{v}_B​, is directed from West to East. The relative velocity of A with respect to B is given by: v⃗AB=v⃗A−v⃗B{v}_{AB} = {v}_A - {v}_B​ Since vector subtraction can be understood as adding the opposite of the vector, we need to find the direction of v⃗A{v}_A​ relative to −v⃗B-{v}_B− (which would be the opposite direction of B's velocity, so East to West). Now, when we subtract v⃗B{v}_B​ from v⃗A{v}_A: v⃗A{v}_A is directed North. −v⃗B-{v}_B−​ is directed West. The resultant vector v⃗AB{v}_{AB} B​ will therefore be directed in a diagonal line combining North and West, which points towards North-West. Correct answer: Option A (North-West).

questions.question: Which of the following position-time graphs correctly represents two moving objects A and B with zero relative velocity?
questions.explanation: Relative velocity is defined as the velocity of one object as observed from another object. If two objects have zero relative velocity, it means they are moving at the same velocity. The slope of a position-time graph indicates the velocity of the object.- If two objects have the same slope, they have the same velocity. Graph 1: Check if the slopes of lines representing objects A and B are equal.- If both slopes are equal, then the velocities are equal, indicating zero relative velocity. Graph 2: Check the slopes of A and B.- If the slopes are different, then the velocities are not equal, indicating non-zero relative velocity.Graph 3: Repeat the slope check for A and B.- Again, if the slopes differ, the relative velocity is not zero.Graph 4: Check the slopes of A and B.- If the slopes are different, the relative velocity is not zero. After analyzing all four graphs:- If Graph 1 shows equal slopes for both A and B, then this graph represents zero relative velocity.- The other graphs (2, 3, and 4) show different slopes, indicating non-zero relative velocities. Thus, the correct answer is Graph 1.

questions.question: An object A is moving with 10 {~m} / {s} and B is moving with 5 {~m} / {s} in the same direction of positive x -axis. A is 100 {~m} behind B as shown. Find time taken by A to meet {B} .
questions.explanation: Both objects move in the same direction along a straight line: vA=10v_A = 10 m/s vB=5v_B = 5 m/s Initial separation = 100 m Time for A to catch B is given by the initial gap (100 m)(100\,{m}) divided by the relative speed (10−5=5 m/s)(10 - 5=5\,{m/s}). Hence, t=1005=20 s.t = 100/5 = 20\,{s}.

questions.question: A ball A is dropped from a building of height 45 m. Simultaneously another identical ball B is thrown up with a speed 50 ms–1. The relative speed of ball B w.r.t. ball A at any instant of time till both balls are in air is (Take g = 10 ms–2)
questions.explanation: Let upward be the positive direction. Velocity of A (dropped from rest): vA(t)=− g t=− 10 t.v_A(t) = -\,g\,t = -\,10\,t. Velocity of B (thrown up at 50 m/s): vB(t)=+ 50−10 t.v_B(t) = +\,50 - 10\,t. Relative velocity of B w.r.t. A: vB∣A(t)  =  vB(t)−vA(t)=[ 50−10t]−[−10t]=50. v_{B|A}(t) \;=\; v_B(t) - v_A(t) = [\,50 - 10t] - [-10t] = 50. Since that difference is always 50 m/s, the relative speed remains 50 m/s at every instant.

questions.question: Preeti reached the metro station and found that the escalator was not working. She walked up the stationary escalator in time t1. On other days, if she remains stationary on the moving escalator, then the escalator takes her up in time t2. The time taken by her to walk up on the moving escalator will be:
questions.explanation: Let: Escalator length = LL Preeti’s walking speed = vp=Lt1v_p = L/t_1 Escalator speed = ve=Lt2v_e = L/t_2 When both move together (Preeti walks on moving escalator): Net speed = vp+ve=L/tv_p + v_e = L/t ⇒L/t=Lt1+Lt2⇒1/t=1t1+1t2⇒t=t1t2t1+t2 L/t = L/t_1 + L/t_2 1/t = 1/t_1 + 1/t_2 t = t_1 t_2/t_1 + t_2

questions.question: A person sitting in an open car moving at constant velocity throws a ball vertically up into air. The ball falls:
options: In the car ahead of the person
In the car to the side of the person
Exactly in the hand which threw it up
questions.explanation: There is no relative motion between person and ball in horizontal direction. So the ball falls in hand of the person.

questions.question: Two cars are moving in the same direction with a speed of 30 km/h. They are separated from each other by 5 km. Third car moving in the opposite direction meets the two cars after an interval of 4 minutes. The speed of the third car is
questions.explanation: Let the two eastbound cars each have speed 30 km/h, separated by 5 km. A third car goes west at speed v v. The time difference between meeting the two cars is 4 minutes = 115 hr {1}{15}\,{hr}. Meet first car ⇒ relative speed = v+30 v + 30; separation 5 km. Meet second car ⇒ time differs by 115 hr {1}{15}\,{hr}. Hence, in that 115 hr {1}{15}\,{hr}, the westbound car covers the extra 5 km at the same relative speed (v+30)(v + 30). So: (v+30)⋅115=5⟹v+30=75⟹v=45.(v+30) {1}{15} = 5 v + 30 = 75 v = 45.

questions.question: Two cars {A} and {B} are moving in same direction with velocities 30 {~m} / {s} and 20 {~m} / {s} respectively. When car A is at a distance d behind the car {B} , the driver of the car {A} applies brakes producing uniform retardation of 2 {m} / {s}² . There will be no collision when
Two trains each of length 100 {~m} moving parallel towards each other at speed 72 {~km} / {h} and 36 {~km} / {h} respectively. In how much time will they cross each other?
A ball is dropped from the top of a building of height 80 m. At same instant another ball is thrown upwards with speed 50 m/s from the bottom of the building. The time at which balls will meet is
questions.explanation: Set origin at the building’s bottom. Ball from top (height 80 m), dropped with initial velocity 0: yA(t)=80−12 g t²=80−4.9 t².y_A(t) = 80 - 12\,g\,t² = 80 - 4.9\,t². Ball from bottom with initial velocity 50 m/s upward: yB(t)=0+50 t−4.9 t².y_B(t) = 0 + 50\,t - 4.9\,t². At collision, yA(t)=yB(t)y_A(t) = y_B(t): 80−4.9t²=50t−4.9t²⟹80=50t⟹t=8050=1.6 s.80 - 4.9t² = 50t - 4.9t² 80 = 50t t = 80/50 = 1.6\,{s}.

questions.question: Shown in the figure are the displacement time graph for two children going home from the school. Which of the following statements about their relative motion is true after both of them started moving? Their relative velocity:
questions.explanation: From the given displacement–time plot, each child’s graph is a straight line with a distinct constant slope. That means each child moves with a constant (but different) velocity once they start. Consequently, their relative velocity is the constant difference of these two constant velocities. Hence, their relative velocity is a nonzero constant.

questions.question: At an instant t, the co-ordinates of a particle are x = at2, y = bt2 and z = 0, then its velocity at the instant t will be

Then the velocity components are: vx=dxdt=2 a t,vy=dydt=2 b t,vz=0.v_x = dx/dt = 2\,a\,t, v_y = dy/dt = 2\,b\,t, v_z=0. Hence, the speed is v=(2 a t)2+(2 b t)2=2 t a²+b².v = √{(2\,a\,t)² + (2\,b\,t)² = 2\,t\,√{a² + b².

questions.question: Two particles A and B, move with constant velocities {v}_{1} and {v}_{2} . At the initial moment their position vector {P} are {r}_{1} and {r}_{2} respectively. The condition for particles A and {B} for their collision is:
questions.explanation: For particles AA and BB to collide, they must occupy the same position at some time tt. In vector form: r1+v1 t  =  r2+v2 t⟹r1−r2  =  (v2−v1) t.{r}_1 + {v}_1\,t \;=\;{r}_2 + {v}_2\,t {r}_1 - {r}_2 \;=\;({v}_2 - {v}_1)\,t. For a real (and positive) solution tt to exist, the vector r1−r2{r}_1 - {r}_2 must be parallel (or anti‑parallel) to the relative‑velocity vector v2−v1{v}_2 - {v}_1. In normalized form, this collinearity condition is: r1−r2∣r1−r2∣  =  v2−v1∣v2−v1∣.

questions.question: As shown in figure, the particle B is south of A at a distance d . They start moving simultaneously, such that A moves with constant speed v towards east and B with constant speed v towards north. Find the minimum separation between them.
questions.explanation: Let A(t)=(vt, 0)A(t) = (vt,\,0) B(t)=(0, vt−d)B(t) = (0,\,vt-d) Then, D²=(vt)2+(vt−d)2=2v²t²−2dv t+d².D² = (vt)² + (vt-d)² = 2v²t² - 2dv\,t + d². Minimizing: ddt(D²)=4v²t−2dv=0⇒t=d2v.d/dt(D²) = 4v²t - 2dv = 0 t = d/2v. Substitute back: Dmin⁡2=2v²(d2v)2−2dv(d2v)+d²=d²2,D_{}² = 2v²(d/2v)² - 2dv(d/2v) + d² = d²/2, Dmin⁡=d2.D_{} = d/√(2).

questions.question: A student is standing at a distance of 50 metres from the bus. Assuming the motion to be along a straight road, the minimum value of u, so that the student is able to catch the bus is:

Then A “catches” B in time tt found from relative speed  (20−10)=10 m/s.\,(20 - 10)=10\,{m/s}. t  =  40010  =  40 s.t \;=\;400/10 \;=\;40\,{s}.

questions.question: Find relative velocity of B w.r.t. A
Ball A is projected downward with speed 10 m/s and ball B is dropped from same height then separation between them after 2 sec
questions.explanation: Let downward be the positive direction. Ball A (projected downward at 10 m/s): yA=u t+12 g t²  =  10 t+5 t².y_A = u\,t + 12\,g\,t² \;=\;10\,t + 5\,t². At t=2t=2,s, yA=10×2+5×(22)=20+20=40y_A = 102 + 5(2²) = 20+20=40 m. Ball B (dropped, u=0u=0): yB=0 ⋅ t+12 g t²=5 t².y_B = 0\,\,t + 12\,g\,t² = 5\,t². At t=2t=2,s, yB=5×4=20y_B = 54=20 m. Separation = yA−yB=40−20=20y_A - y_B = 40 - 20 = 20 m.

A helicopter is flying south with a speed of 50 {kmh}^{-1} . A train is moving with the same speed towards east. The relative velocity of the helicopter as seen by the passengers in the train will be towards.
questions.explanation: Assign east as +x and north as +y. Helicopter: vheli=(0, −50) km/hv_{{heli}} = (0,\,-50)\,{km/h} Train: vtrain=(50, 0) km/hv_{{train}} = (50,\,0)\,{km/h} Relative velocity of helicopter w.r.t. train: vheli/train=vheli−vtrain=(0−50, −50−0)=(−50, −50).v_{{heli/train}} = v_{{heli}} - v_{{train}} = (0-50,\,-50-0) = (-50,\,-50). This vector points 50{50} km/h west and 50{50} km/h south ⇒ south‐west direction.

questions.question: A boat is sent across a river with a velocity of 8 {km} / {hr} . If the resultant velocity of boat is 10 {~km} / {hr} , then velocity of the river is:
questions.explanation: Boat’s velocity in still water = 8 km/h (perpendicular to current)Resultant velocity = 10 km/h By Pythagoras on the velocity triangle, (river speed)2+82=102  ⇒  (river speed)2=100−64=36  ⇒  river speed=6 km/h.({river speed})² + 8² = 10² \;\; ({river speed})² = 100 - 64 = 36 \;\; {river speed} = 6 \,{km/h}.

questions.question: The stream of a river is flowing with a speed of 2 km/h. A swimmer can swim at a speed of 4 km/h. What should be the direction of the swimmer with respect to the flow of the river to cross the river straight ?
questions.explanation: Label the river flow along the positive xx‐axis at 2 km/h. The swimmer’s own speed (relative to the water) is 4 km/h at some angle θ measured from the direction of the flow. To cross straight over, the net xx‐component of the swimmer’s ground‐frame velocity must be zero: vnet,x  =  vriver+vswimcos⁡θ  =  0.v_{{net},x} \;=\; v_{{river}} + v_{{swim}} \;=\;0. That is, 2+4 cos⁡θ  =  0  ⟹  cos⁡θ=−12  ⟹  θ=120∘.2 + 4\, \;=\;0 \;\; = -12 \;\; =120^.

Horizontal driftIn the ground frame, the river current carries the boat downstream at 22 km/h. Thus in 0.050.05 hr, drift  =  2×0.05  =  0.1  km  =  100  m. {drift} \;=\;2 0.05 \;=\;0.1\;{km} \;=\;100\;{m}.

questions.question: A man standing on a road hold his umbrella at 30^{} with the vertical to keep the rain away. He throws the umbrella and starts running at 10 {~km} / {hr} . He finds that raindrops are hitting his head vertically, the speed of raindrops with respect to the road will be
questions.explanation: Initial condition (man is standing):The rain appears at 30∘30^ from the vertical. If (Vx, Vy)(V_x,\,V_y) is the rain’s true velocity (ground frame, with Vy>0V_y>0 downward), then tan⁡30∘  =  VxVy  =  13⟹Vx=Vy3. 30^ \;=\;V_x/V_y \;=\;1/√(3) V_x = V_y/√(3). After the man runs at 10 km/h horizontally:He sees raindrops hitting vertically, i.e. the relative velocity has no horizontal component. The man’s velocity is (10, 0)(10,\,0). So (Vx−10,  Vy)    is purely vertical⟹Vx=10. (V_x - 10,\;V_y)\;\;{is purely vertical} V_x = 10. Combine both conditions:From step 1 and step 2: Vx=10andVx=Vy3⟹Vy=10 3. V_x=10 {and} V_x=V_y/√(3) V_y=10\,√(3). Resultant speed of the rain (ground frame): V=(10)2+(103)2  =  100+300  =  20 km/h. V=√((10)² + (10√{3))² \;=\;√(100 + 300) \;=\;20{ km/h}.

questions.question: A standing man observes rain falling with velocity of 20 {~m} / {s} at an angle of 30^{} with the vertical. Find the velocity with which the man should move so that rain appears to fall vertically to him.
questions.explanation: Rain’s speed = 20 m/s, directed 30∘30^ from vertical. Decompose: Vertical component = 20cos⁡(30∘)=20×32=103 m/s20(30^)=20{√(3)}{2}=10√(3)\,{m/s}. Horizontal component = 20sin⁡(30∘)=20×12=10 m/s.20(30^)=2012=10\,{m/s}. For the man to see the rain vertical, the rain’s horizontal component relative to him must be zero. Hence the man’s horizontal velocity must match the rain’s horizontal component (10 m/s).

questions.question: Rain is falling vertically downwards with a velocity of 3 {~km} / {hr} . A man walks in the rain with a velocity of 4 {~km} / {hr} . The raindrops will fall on the man with a velocity (in magnitude) of
questions.explanation: Let the rain's velocity (ground frame) be v⃗r=(0, −3)(km/hr),{v}_r = (0,\,-3) {(km/hr)}, and the man's velocity be v⃗m=(4, 0).{v}_m = (4,\,0). The rain's velocity relative to the man is: v⃗rm=v⃗r−v⃗m=(−4, −3).{v}_{rm} = {v}_r - {v}_m = (-4,\,-3). Its magnitude is: ∣v⃗rm∣=(−4)2+(−3)2=16+9=5 km/hr.|{v}_{rm}| = √((-4)² + (-3)² = √{16+9) = 5\ {km/hr}. Thus, the raindrops fall on the man with a velocity of 5 km/hr.

questions.question: To a stationary man, rain appears to be falling at an angle 30^{} with the vertical. As he starts moving with a speed of 0.5 {~m} / {s} he finds that the rain is falling vertically. Then the speed of rain w.r.t. the moving man is:
questions.explanation: Set up velocities in the ground frame Let the rain’s velocity be (Vx, Vy)(V_x,\,V_y) with Vy>0V_y>0 downward. Initially, the man is stationary; he sees rain at 30∘30^ from vertical  ⟹  tan⁡30∘=VxVy=13 30^ = {V_x}{V_y} = {1}{√(3)}, so Vx  =  Vy3. V_x \;=\;V_y/√(3). Condition for vertical appearance When the man starts walking horizontally at 0.50.5 m/s, the rain appears vertical to him  ⟹   the relative horizontal component (Vx−0.5)(V_x - 0.5) is zero. Hence, Vx  =  0.5. V_x \;=\;0.5. Find vertical speed of rainFrom step 1, Vx=Vy3=0.5V_x={V_y}{√(3)}=0.5, so Vy=0.5 3. V_y=0.5\,√(3). Speed of rain w.r.t. moving man Relative velocity of rain = (Vx−0.5,  Vy)  =  (0, 0.5 3)(V_x-0.5,\;V_y)\;=\;(0,\,0.5\,√(3)). Magnitude = 0.5 3 m/s.0.5\,√(3)\,{m/s}.

A boat takes 2 hours to go 8 km and come back in still water lake. The time taken for going 8 km upstream and coming back with water velocity of 4km/h is:
questions.explanation: (3) Speed in still water:The boat covers 8 km forth and 8 km back in still water in 2 hours. Total time  =  8/v+8/v  =  16/v=2⟹v=8 km/h.{Total time} \;=\; 8/v + 8/v \;=\; 16/v = 2 v=8\,{km/h}. With river flow:Let the water’s flow be 4 km/h.4\,{km/h}. Upstream speed =  8−4=4 km/h=\;8-4=4\,{km/h}. Downstream speed =  8+4=12 km/h=\;8+4=12\,{km/h}. Time upstream = 84{8}{4}=2 h;time downstream=812{8}{12}=2323 h=40 min. Hence the total round‐trip time is 2 h+40 min=160 min.2\,{h}+40\,{min}={160\,{min}}.

questions.question: A person swims in a river aiming to reach exactly on the opposite point on the bank of a river. His speed of swimming is 0.5 m/s at an angle of 120° with the direction of flow of water. The speed of water is
questions.explanation: (3) Set up a coordinate system with the river flowing along the xx‐axis. The swimmer has: Speed relative to water: 0.5 m/s Direction: 120° from the river flow (i.e.\ 120° from the +x+x‐axis) Let the water‐flow speed be vwv_w. Then the swimmer’s xx‐component of velocity relative to the ground is vx,(ground)  =  vw  +  0.5 cos⁡(120∘)  =  vw  +  0.5 (−0.5)  =  vw  −  0.25.v_{x,{(ground)}} \;=\; v_w \;+\; 0.5\,(120^) \;=\; v_w \;+\; 0.5\,(-0.5) \;=\; v_w \;-\; 0.25. To land exactly opposite his starting point, the net xx‐displacement must be zero, so this xx‐component must be zero: vw  −  0.25  =  0⟹vw=0.25 m/s.v_w \;-\;0.25 \;=\;0 v_w=0.25{ m/s}.

questions.question: The motion of one projectile as seen from another will always be
questions.explanation: (1) Both projectiles experience the same uniform gravitational acceleration. Hence, their relative acceleration is zero, and so their relative velocity is constant. Therefore, as viewed from one projectile, the other moves in a straight line.
